clue.text: Hit Parade EP entered

indicators.note: something hit is knocked about, so the letters of the next two words are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A record, an extended-play single, made its debut in the Hit Parade, the old pop chart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit Parade' reads as one phrase, the chart, but 'Hit' is the anagram signal working on PARADE and EP together.
explanation.definitionFit: To have come onstage or into view is to have entered, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Row abated finally after seaman embarked

indicators.note: after places the rowing piece and the last letter behind the sailor

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is the usual crossword sailor
to row a boat you pull an oar, the noun for the thing rowed with

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word abated

explanation.surface: Once the storm abated, a sailor finally went back on board his ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has embarked is now on the ship, which is the adverb's sense of being on board.

clue.text: Model veils hype in a petulant way

indicators.note: to model is to shape or fashion, so the letters of veils and hype are fashioned into a new word

explanation.surface: A catwalk model turns sulky about the veils and all the hype surrounding the show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' looks like the subject of the sentence; it is the instruction to rearrange VEILS HYPE.
explanation.definitionFit: Peevish and petulant are synonyms for irritable sulkiness, so the adverbs match.

clue.text: Without secrets now and then local newspaper may give up agony aunt?

indicators.note: without asks for the named letters to be taken out of the newspaper's title

parts.note: many British local papers carry the title Advertiser, as in the Croydon Advertiser

indicators.note: now and then picks every other letter of secrets, starting from the second

explanation.surface: A local paper with no secrets left to share might drop its agony aunt column.
explanation.walkthrough: 'now and then' gives the even letters E, R, T of secrets; take those out of ADVERTISER. The question mark flags that an agony aunt is one kind of adviser.
explanation.definitionFit: An agony aunt is a newspaper columnist who counsels readers, an example of someone giving guidance.

clue.text: Unnatural note with English — not British — cheese

parts.note: E is one of the musical notes A to G

indicators.note: not means the letter for British is left out of the cheese

parts.note: Brie is a soft French cheese

explanation.surface: A tasting note describes a strange-tasting English cheese, carefully labelled as not British.
explanation.definitionFit: Something eerie is uncanny or supernatural, so it can fairly be called unnatural.

clue.text: One goes spare being out around very loud clubs

indicators.note: around says the word out wraps round the other letters

parts.note: FF, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: Someone goes mad after a night out round very loud nightclubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes spare' is British slang for losing one's temper, but here it means a piece left over.
explanation.definitionFit: An offcut is a leftover scrap of wood, cloth or paper, the bit that becomes spare after cutting.

clue.text: Iris is complimentary on most of old Eastern country

parts.note: complimentary tickets are free of charge

indicators.note: most of means the old country's name loses its final letter

parts.note: Siam is the former name of Thailand

explanation.surface: Someone named Iris pays a compliment about a former Asian kingdom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iris' looks like a woman's name; it is the flower family the answer belongs to.
explanation.definitionFit: The freesia is a fragrant flowering plant of the iris family, so it is an example of an iris.

clue.text: Disastrous upset — no time for celebratory smoke

indicators.note: no means the letter for time is dropped
upset in a down clue turns the word for disastrous upside down, reading it backwards

parts.note: a disastrous event is a tragic one

explanation.surface: After a disastrous defeat, there is no time for any victory cigar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns TRAGIC into CIGART; 'no time' removes the T.
explanation.definitionFit: Cigars are traditionally handed out or lit to mark a birth or a win, hence a smoke for celebrating.

clue.text: Article on temperature in Times gutlessly went amiss in rags

indicators.note: on places the article directly after the temperature letter

parts.note: A is the indefinite article
T stands for time, so two Ts make times, plural

indicators.note: gutlessly says the middle letter of the word for went amiss is removed

parts.note: to go amiss is to err, so went amiss is erred

explanation.surface: A newspaper article about temperatures went wrong and the Times was left in shreds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gutlessly' takes the central R out of ERRED to leave ERED. TT for 'Times' is the plural of T for time.
explanation.definitionFit: Tattered clothing is ragged and torn, so the wearer is dressed in rags.

clue.text: Hypocritical person is a peer surprisingly — hard to figure

indicators.note: to figure is to feature or appear in, so the letter for hard appears among the rearranged letters
surprisingly signals that is a peer comes out in an unexpected order

parts.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A member of the House of Lords turns out, surprisingly, to be a difficult man to read.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard to figure' reads as puzzling; it means H is to feature in the rearranged IS A PEER.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pharisees of the Gospels are condemned as self-righteous, so the word now means a sanctimonious hypocrite.

clue.text: Half-cut boxer who's unfit to fight without whisky

indicators.note: without says the letter for whisky is taken away

parts.note: a boxer above the limit for his class at the weigh-in is over the weight and cannot fight
Whisky is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for W

explanation.surface: A drunken boxer is in no state to fight unless he gives up the whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk. Taking W from WEIGHT leaves EIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom for a drink too many describes someone slightly drunk, which is what half-cut means.

clue.text: Queen's about to encounter controversy, one that's circulating again

indicators.note: about turns the Queen's two letters round

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's royal cipher
an issue is a matter in dispute, a controversy

explanation.surface: The Queen is about to run into some controversy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' reads as 'on the point of'; 'about' is the reversal and 'to encounter' joins.
explanation.definitionFit: A book or record put out a second time is a reissue, a new edition sent into circulation.

clue.text: Stock put back on plate?

definitions.meaning: a stock kept back for future use
to serve food again, read as ..., is to put it back on the plate

explanation.surface: Stock soup returned to the plate.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word as re-serve; the question mark flags the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A reserve is a supply held back, a stockpile; split, the word means serve again.

clue.text: Church processions showing lack of power games in party?

indicators.note: showing lack of says the letter for power is missing from the processions

parts.note: parades are processions
P is the physics abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: Church parades lack the energy of party games.
explanation.definitionFit: Charades is a guessing game acted out at parties, an example of party games.

clue.text: With the exception of a masked duo cast landed parts

indicators.note: with the exception of says one letter, a, is excluded from the letter pool
cast means thrown into a new shape, so the remaining letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Apart from a pair in masks, the cast all landed parts in the play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'landed parts' reads as actors getting roles; it is territory held by nobles. Remove A from MASKED DUO and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A dukedom is the territory ruled by a duke, so such estates are landed parts of a realm.

clue.text: Ring for Charlie among principal letters for residential property

indicators.note: for means one letter stands in place of the other within the run

parts.note: the first five letters of the alphabet are the principal or leading ones
Charlie is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for C
a ring is round, like the letter O

explanation.surface: An estate agent rings about a home on a prime street.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ABCDE and swap its C for O.
explanation.definitionFit: An abode is a dwelling or home, which is a property people live in.

clue.text: Responsibility for lapse

definitions.meaning: supervision, the duty of watching over something

explanation.definitionFit: The word holds both meanings: supervising a job and failing to notice a mistake.

clue.text: Possibly bitter about one in clan breaking up marriage?

indicators.note: about says the beer goes round the other letters

parts.note: bitter is a kind of beer, an ale

indicators.note: in places the numeral inside the rearranged clan
breaking up shows the letters of clan broken apart and reassembled

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Bitter feelings about one member of a clan threaten to break up a marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks marriage as one example of an alliance.
explanation.definitionFit: A union of families by marriage is an alliance, a word for any close partnership or pact.

clue.text: Film in Dorking or Orpington?

definitions.meaning: a thin film over a surface is a coating, one stratum
Dorking and Orpington are breeds of hen, kept for egg-laying

explanation.surface: A movie set in two towns in south-east England.
explanation.walkthrough: Dorking and Orpington are towns south of London, but both also name breeds of chicken.
explanation.definitionFit: A layer is a thin sheet of material, and also a hen kept for its eggs.

clue.text: Stories concerning tantrum coming up

parts.note: re means concerning, as in a letter heading

indicators.note: coming up in a down clue means the word rises, read bottom to top

parts.note: a strop is British slang for a fit of bad temper

explanation.surface: Stories about a celebrity tantrum are emerging.
explanation.definitionFit: Reports are news accounts, the items journalists file as stories.

clue.text: Born Democrat taken in by backward glance but a long way from out of his depth

definitions.text: a long way from out of his depth

indicators.note: taken in by says the born and Democrat letters go inside the reversed glance
backward means the word for glance is read in reverse

parts.note: a peek is a quick glance
nee, French for born, introduces a maiden name

explanation.surface: A Democrat newcomer, given a backward glance, is far from being out of his depth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' gives KEEP. The definition is literal: water up to the knees is shallow, though the idiom usually means deeply involved.
explanation.definitionFit: Water reaching only to the knees is shallow, nowhere near over one's head.

clue.text: Fiasco as the Spanish half-heartedly took a taxi heading north

indicators.note: heading north in a down clue means the letters are read upwards, in reverse

parts.note: el is Spanish for the

indicators.note: half-heartedly means one of the two central letters is lost

parts.note: to cab is to travel by taxi, so took a taxi is cabbed

explanation.surface: A Spanish taxi ride, taken without enthusiasm, ends in disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-heartedly' drops one B of CABBED; 'heading north' reverses ELCABED.
explanation.definitionFit: A debacle is a complete and humiliating failure, which is what a fiasco is.

clue.text: Tarry rope attached

parts.note: a stay is a rope supporting a ship's mast
on means attached, as a lid is on

explanation.surface: A rope coated in tar, fixed in place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tarry' reads as an adjective, covered in tar; it is the verb to linger.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarry is to linger or remain behind, the sense of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Touring Sweden, I dip in crackers with bland flavour

indicators.note: touring means going round, so the rearranged letters go round the Swedish letter
crackers means crazy, so I dip in goes mad and reshuffles

parts.note: S is the international vehicle code for Sweden

explanation.surface: On a trip round Sweden, a tourist dips crackers into a rather tasteless dip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crackers' looks like biscuits; it is the anagram signal for I DIP IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Insipid food lacks taste, so it has a bland flavour.

clue.text: Rising French creator of novel spice

indicators.note: rising in a down clue means the writer's name is read upwards

parts.note: Albert Camus was a French novelist, author of The Outsider

explanation.surface: An up-and-coming French novelist creates a spicy new book.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground sumac berries make a tart red seasoning used in Middle Eastern cooking.

clue.text: It's unending hell checking mite, mind

indicators.note: checking means holding back, so the word for hell sits inside the small amount, blocking it

parts.note: a mite is a small bit, a tiny amount

indicators.note: unending says the word for hell loses its final letter

parts.note: the abyss is the bottomless pit of hell

explanation.surface: Looking after a tiny child is never-ending hell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mite' looks like a small child; it is a small amount, BIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To mind children for their parents is to look after them while the parents are out.

clue.text: Piece of furniture one found in flowerpot with companion

parts.note: Bill and Ben the Flowerpot Men were puppets in a British children's TV show, living in flowerpots
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British award

explanation.surface: A garden seat and a flowerpot, with a friend alongside.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill and Ben the Flowerpot Men is a 1950s British children's programme; Ben is one of the pair.
explanation.definitionFit: A bench is a long seat, which is an item of furniture.

clue.text: Ignore one crummy drunk's response to being taken advantage of?

definitions.text: response to being taken advantage of?

indicators.note: drunk's, short for drunk is, says the letters are tipsy and reel into a new order

explanation.surface: A drunk tells you to ignore some lousy person.
explanation.definitionFit: The catchphrase announces that someone exploited too often will stop being kind, a typical reaction to being used.

clue.text: Space suit gives cover

parts.note: an en is a printer's unit of space
a case is a lawsuit, a suit at law

explanation.surface: An astronaut's spacesuit covers him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Space suit' reads as one thing; it is two pieces, EN and CASE.
explanation.definitionFit: To encase something is to enclose it fully, the same as covering it.

clue.text: Bully using web the wrong way to nurse broken heart

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, so the reversed web holds the rearranged heart inside
the wrong way means the word for web runs backwards

parts.note: a net is a web of mesh

indicators.note: broken says the letters of heart are smashed and rearranged

explanation.surface: A cyberbully uses the web to taunt someone whose heart is broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the wrong way' turns NET into TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: To bully someone is to intimidate them, and to threaten is the same kind of menacing.
